metricGrades.observedResult: On the 580-patient randomized double-blind ABTECT-Maintenance exact-trial Phase 3 readout, Week-44 clinical remission occurred in 98/193 (50.8%) at 25mg and 100/195 (51.3%) at 50mg versus 20/192 (10.4%) placebo. Sponsor reports stratification-adjusted placebo differences 39.3 and 40.3 percentage points with both p<0.0001. Observed current results, not predictions.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: The prospective randomized ABTECT-Maintenance control is 20/192 (10.4%) Week-44 clinical remission; both active arms exceeded placebo by about 39–40 percentage points. Published TRUE NORTH ozanimod maintenance trial had 37.0% versus 18.5% (18.5 percentage points). This published cross-program context is NOT a head-to-head benchmark; differences in patient selection and trial timing prevent any claim of therapeutic superiority.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: The readout is issuer-reported (SEC-filed), detailed prespecified effect confidence intervals, full SAP, ascertainment, and handling of missing data are not fully independently verified. Patients were induction responders re-randomized for maintenance; this is not efficacy in all initiating patients. Cross-program comparator is contextual only.

metricGrades.observedResult: At ABTECT-Maintenance Week 44, endoscopic remission was 41.5% (25mg) and 47.7% (50mg) versus placebo 9.9%; corticosteroid-free clinical remission was 45.1% and 47.7% versus 9.9%; sustained clinical remission among remission-at-induction subgroups was 67.1% and 65.6% versus 15.7%. All reported p<0.0001 in issuer SEC exhibit.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Clinically meaningful UC benefit is defined using validated clinical remission, endoscopic healing and corticosteroid-free remission rather than p-values alone. The published GEMINI 1 randomized maintenance study used clinical remission and mucosal healing as relevant patient-oriented disease-control endpoints. Different programs and populations cannot establish relative drug ranking.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: These are clinically meaningful mucosal and steroid-free measurements, but original public topline lacks complete patient-reported quality-of-life score tables, full multiplicity-adjusted confidence intervals and adjudicated missing-data analyses. Sustained remission compares selected induction remitters.

metricGrades.observedResult: ABTECT-Maintenance randomized 580 initial induction responders (placebo 192, 25mg 193, 50mg 195), reporting Week-44 clinical remission 10.4%, 50.8% and 51.3% with stratification-adjusted placebo differences 39.3 and 40.3 points, both p<0.0001; multiplicity and conservative missing-outcome scenarios are not supplied in full SEC summary.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: TRUE NORTH reported randomized maintenance remission comparisons and prespecified hierarchical outcomes. The ABTECT 6-K reports adjusted risk differences using Mantel-Haenszel stratification (baseline remission, induction dose and corticosteroid use) with nominal reported p<0.0001 across primary and key secondary endpoints. This is encouraging but does not disclose all analytic details needed to independently test multiplicitiy and missing-data sensitivity.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Reported p-values and predeclared stratification are not substitutes for accessible final SAP, confidence intervals for all contrasts, imputation, sensitivity analyses or an independently reanalysed dataset. Applicant-controlled topline is the source, so robustness is not fully established.

metricGrades.observedResult: ABTECT-Maintenance randomized 580 induction responders across 25mg, 50mg and placebo and found Week-44 clinical remission near 51% in both doses versus 10.4% placebo. Sponsor also reports sustained clinical remission among Week-8 remission subgroups 67.1% and 65.6% vs 15.7% placebo. Separate prior induction trials demonstrated consistent 50mg benefit; 25mg induction was less consistent.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Prior ABTECT-1 and ABTECT-2 randomized induction datasets met their Week-8 clinical-remission primary endpoint for the 50mg arms (ABTECT-1 21.7% vs 2.5% placebo, ABTECT-2 19.8% vs 6.3%). ABTECT-2 25mg clinical-remission contrast was not significant (p=0.1034). These are two distinct induction trials but NOT randomized replication of Week-44 maintenance.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Maintenance durability is measured in a selected responder population; the maintenance phase itself has no separate blinded confirmatory maintenance study in these sources. Induction and maintenance outcomes involve different populations/endpoints. Long-term 7-year extension described by sponsor is uncontrolled and not independent replication.

metricGrades.observedResult: SEC-hosted ABTECT-Maintenance arm table (placebo n192, 25mg n193, 50mg n195): any TEAE 50.0%,58.0%,71.8%; serious TEAE 4.2%,2.6%,5.6%; study-drug discontinuations due to TEAE 6.8%,2.6%,4.6%; deaths 0 all groups. Serious/severe infection events reported 1.0%,1.0%,0.5%. Non-melanoma skin cancers 1 in placebo and 3 each in 25/50mg arms; single cases of prostate, breast and dysplasia in 50mg with attribution uncertain.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: TRUE NORTH maintenance reported infection rates higher with ozanimod than placebo but serious infection under 2%, furnishing an illustrative UC maintenance treatment setting, not direct head-to-head safety comparison. ABTECT's own placebo arm is primary safety comparator for treatment-emergent events and discontinuations.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Dose-related increase in any TEAE (50mg 71.8% vs placebo 50%) counters a uniformly favorable safety claim. Serious event counts are small and uncommon outcomes underpowered; trial selection limits generalizability. Attribution of skin cancers and longer exposure risk not established by topline.

metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Pre-existing international NTDT-thalassemia management guidance identifies a sustained hemoglobin increase of at least 1 g/dL as a clinically relevant therapeutic objective in symptomatic patients.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Published randomized controlled trial and CI support clear relative hemoglobin effect; 24-week primary observation, larger-term liver safety, REMS and posttrial benefit-risk cannot be assumed from this source.

metricGrades.observedResult: Peer-reviewed ENERGIZE randomized non-transfusion-dependent thalassemia trial: hemoglobin response 55/130 (42%) vs 1/64 (2%), adjusted absolute difference approximately 41 percentage points (95% CI 32–50), two-sided p<0.0001. 7 treatment-arm participants and 1 placebo participant stopped study treatment before week 24.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: FDA's ICH E9(R1) final statistical guidance and Multiple Endpoints final guidance require carefully defined estimands and credible multiplicity/sensitivity evaluations. This independent regulatory methodology benchmark is not an FDA judgment about this trial.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: A well-defined binary primary endpoint and confidence interval are documented, but published abstract alone does not establish all SAP estimands, sensitivity under missing data or multiplicity for secondary fatigue/functional endpoints; one should not infer liver safety robustness from efficacy statistical strength.

metricGrades.observedResult: Conference abstract O33 with exact NCT04770753: 182 entered OLE, 121 continuing mitapivat, 61 crossover; among 55 original randomized responders mean Hb response duration 17.9 (SD3.6) weeks within double-blind period versus 43.6 (SD24.2) weeks cumulatively through OLE. Seventy-two of 121 (59.5%) originally active-treated achieved an OLE Hb response and some lasted up to 93.3 weeks.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Randomized 24-week ENERGIZE NCT04770753 produced hemoglobin response 55/130 (42%) mitapivat versus 1/64 (2%) placebo, 41 percentage point adjusted difference, 95% CI 32–50. Later open-label extension is a distinct post-hoc, uncontrolled and selected survivor cohort, not an independent pivotal replicate.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: OLE lacked placebo comparator, enrollment selected DB completers, includes post-hoc responder classification, different follow-up exposure (median 71 weeks active-active vs 44 weeks placebo-active) and potential informative dropout. Longer period is encouraging for persistence but uncertain for causal replication.

metricGrades.observedResult: Peer-reviewed ENERGIZE randomized NTD thalassemia trial: treatment-emergent events in 107/129 (83%) mitapivat vs 50/63 (79%) placebo. Headache occurred in 29/129 (22%) versus 6/63 (10%); initial insomnia 18/129 (14%) versus 3/63 (5%); nausea 15/129 (12%) versus 5/63 (8%); no deaths. Hemoglobin responders 42% versus 2%. Seven mitapivat and one placebo participants stopped study treatment before week 24; this is not specifically an adverse-event discontinuation count.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Peer-reviewed separate ENERGIZE-T trial of mitapivat in transfusion-dependent, not non-transfusion-dependent, thalassemia provides a safety context (AEs 90% vs 84%), but is not matched same-population active therapy evidence.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: The public abstract does not separately provide all arm-level serious-event and causality categories; the different thalassemia populations cannot be combined to claim head-to-head safety.

metricGrades.observedResult: In peer-reviewed randomized ENERGIZE-T, 238 of 258 (92%) randomized participants completed the double-blind period. At least one qualifying 12-week transfusion-reduction response occurred in 52/171 (30%) mitapivat vs 11/87 (13%) placebo; adjusted difference 18 percentage points (95% CI 8–27), p=0.0003. Its long open-label extension continues and cannot be used as blinded durability replication.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: The September 2026 clinical-trials review confirms a 48-week randomized 2:1 ENERGIZE-T transfusion-reduction study and a planned open-label extension lasting up to five years. Transfusion-reduction response is achieved in ANY consecutive 12-week period, not proof of continuous benefit throughout 48 weeks. Independent placebo-controlled replication or post-extension causal durability is not established by this report.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: The primary 'any 12-week window' response does not establish sustained reduction for each participant across the entire 48-week period. Longer-term observational extension participants are selected and receive no concurrent placebo; results, attrition patterns and long-horizon response trajectories remain incompletely disclosed.

metricGrades.observedResult: Peer-reviewed ENERGIZE-T TDT thalassemia trial: AEs in 155/172 (90%) mitapivat versus 71/85 (84%) placebo; SAEs 19/172 (11%) versus 13/85 (15%), and AE-driven treatment discontinuation 10/172 (6%) versus 1/85 (1%). metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Strong within-trial placebo-adjusted remission does not establish FDA approval or superior efficacy against other UC drugs. Missing full trial report and adverse-event stratification remain material to overall benefit-risk.
metricGrades.observedResult: On the 580-patient randomized double-blind ABTECT-Maintenance exact-trial Phase 3 readout, Week-44 clinical remission occurred in 98/193 (50.8%) at 25mg and 100/195 (51.3%) at 50mg versus 20/192 (10.4%) placebo. Sponsor reports stratification-adjusted placebo differences 39.3 and 40.3 percentage points with both p<0.0001. Observed current results, not predictions.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: The prospective randomized ABTECT-Maintenance control is 20/192 (10.4%) Week-44 clinical remission; both active arms exceeded placebo by about 39–40 percentage points. Published TRUE NORTH ozanimod maintenance trial had 37.0% versus 18.5% (18.5 percentage points). This published cross-program context is NOT a head-to-head benchmark; differences in patient selection and trial timing prevent any claim of therapeutic superiority.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: The readout is issuer-reported (SEC-filed), detailed prespecified effect confidence intervals, full SAP, ascertainment, and handling of missing data are not fully independently verified. Patients were induction responders re-randomized for maintenance; this is not efficacy in all initiating patients. Cross-program comparator is contextual only.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Patient-reported symptoms and long-term function cannot be presumed from endoscopy alone; steroid-free benefit and sustained responses should be checked in full CSR and label. Histologic definitions and protocol changes may matter.
metricGrades.observedResult: At ABTECT-Maintenance Week 44, endoscopic remission was 41.5% (25mg) and 47.7% (50mg) versus placebo 9.9%; corticosteroid-free clinical remission was 45.1% and 47.7% versus 9.9%; sustained clinical remission among remission-at-induction subgroups was 67.1% and 65.6% versus 15.7%. All reported p<0.0001 in issuer SEC exhibit.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Clinically meaningful UC benefit is defined using validated clinical remission, endoscopic healing and corticosteroid-free remission rather than p-values alone. The published GEMINI 1 randomized maintenance study used clinical remission and mucosal healing as relevant patient-oriented disease-control endpoints. Different programs and populations cannot establish relative drug ranking.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: These are clinically meaningful mucosal and steroid-free measurements, but original public topline lacks complete patient-reported quality-of-life score tables, full multiplicity-adjusted confidence intervals and adjudicated missing-data analyses. Sustained remission compares selected induction remitters.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Risk of overconfidence from exceptionally small p-values, responder re-randomization, incomplete ascertainment details, unverified estimand changes or imperfect multiple-comparison adjustment. Missing information is not imputed as an adverse result.
metricGrades.observedResult: ABTECT-Maintenance randomized 580 initial induction responders (placebo 192, 25mg 193, 50mg 195), reporting Week-44 clinical remission 10.4%, 50.8% and 51.3% with stratification-adjusted placebo differences 39.3 and 40.3 points, both p<0.0001; multiplicity and conservative missing-outcome scenarios are not supplied in full SEC summary.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: TRUE NORTH reported randomized maintenance remission comparisons and prespecified hierarchical outcomes. The ABTECT 6-K reports adjusted risk differences using Mantel-Haenszel stratification (baseline remission, induction dose and corticosteroid use) with nominal reported p<0.0001 across primary and key secondary endpoints. This is encouraging but does not disclose all analytic details needed to independently test multiplicitiy and missing-data sensitivity.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Reported p-values and predeclared stratification are not substitutes for accessible final SAP, confidence intervals for all contrasts, imputation, sensitivity analyses or an independently reanalysed dataset. Applicant-controlled topline is the source, so robustness is not fully established.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Do not treat open-label multiyear exposure as independent controlled confirmation or infer durable benefit for induction nonresponders. Full retention, dropout handling, prespecified subgroup interaction tests and maintenance replication remain unresolved.
metricGrades.observedResult: ABTECT-Maintenance randomized 580 induction responders across 25mg, 50mg and placebo and found Week-44 clinical remission near 51% in both doses versus 10.4% placebo. Sponsor also reports sustained clinical remission among Week-8 remission subgroups 67.1% and 65.6% vs 15.7% placebo. Separate prior induction trials demonstrated consistent 50mg benefit; 25mg induction was less consistent.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Prior ABTECT-1 and ABTECT-2 randomized induction datasets met their Week-8 clinical-remission primary endpoint for the 50mg arms (ABTECT-1 21.7% vs 2.5% placebo, ABTECT-2 19.8% vs 6.3%). ABTECT-2 25mg clinical-remission contrast was not significant (p=0.1034). These are two distinct induction trials but NOT randomized replication of Week-44 maintenance.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Maintenance durability is measured in a selected responder population; the maintenance phase itself has no separate blinded confirmatory maintenance study in these sources. Induction and maintenance outcomes involve different populations/endpoints. Long-term 7-year extension described by sponsor is uncontrolled and not independent replication.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Higher 50mg adverse-event burden, rare malignancy imbalances, opportunistic-infection potential and unknown long-term class-specific risks require ongoing surveillance and full safety tables. metricGrades.observedResult: SEC-hosted ABTECT-Maintenance arm table (placebo n192, 25mg n193, 50mg n195): any TEAE 50.0%,58.0%,71.8%; serious TEAE 4.2%,2.6%,5.6%; study-drug discontinuations due to TEAE 6.8%,2.6%,4.6%; deaths 0 all groups. Serious/severe infection events reported 1.0%,1.0%,0.5%. Non-melanoma skin cancers 1 in placebo and 3 each in 25/50mg arms; single cases of prostate, breast and dysplasia in 50mg with attribution uncertain.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: TRUE NORTH maintenance reported infection rates higher with ozanimod than placebo but serious infection under 2%, furnishing an illustrative UC maintenance treatment setting, not direct head-to-head safety comparison. ABTECT's own placebo arm is primary safety comparator for treatment-emergent events and discontinuations.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Dose-related increase in any TEAE (50mg 71.8% vs placebo 50%) counters a uniformly favorable safety claim. Serious event counts are small and uncommon outcomes underpowered; trial selection limits generalizability. Attribution of skin cancers and longer exposure risk not established by topline.

metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Randomized 24-week ENERGIZE NCT04770753 produced hemoglobin response 55/130 (42%) mitapivat versus 1/64 (2%) placebo, 41 percentage point adjusted difference, 95% CI 32–50. metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: The public abstract does not separately provide all arm-level serious-event and causality categories; the different thalassemia populations cannot be combined to claim head-to-head safety.

metricGrades.benchmarkContext: FDA independently confirmed a 4.1-month observed median survival gain and significant PFS in the randomized platinum-resistant ovarian cancer population.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Quality-of-life, symptoms and subjective patient-reported benefit are not established solely by statistically significant all-cause survival; strict entry criteria matter.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Magnitude of treatment response and increased LVEF reductions may alter benefit-risk for a proposed nHCM label; do not interpret two positive P-values as automatic efficacy approval.
metricGrades.observedResult: ACACIA-HCM NCT06081894 enrolled 258 aficamten and 259 placebo patients. At 36 weeks the co-primary pVO2 group difference was +0.67 mL/kg/min (95% CI +0.22 to +1.11; P=0.003); KCCQ-CSS difference +3.0 (95% CI +0.5 to +5.5; P=0.02), each significant at prespecified two-primary alpha <=0.025. Small average effects despite positive prespecified endpoints.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Published HCM anchor estimates are patient-level and developed in a different HCM phenotype from some patients in ACACIA; they cannot turn a mean placebo difference into a patient-level efficacy guarantee or predeclared FDA minimum.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Effect-size lower CI close to zero clinical benefit; no prespecified regulator-endorsed minimum important pVO2 difference in nHCM. Full SAP, imputation and individual response reliability need detailed audit.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Patient importance cannot be established from a group average alone; the proposed nHCM population has no proven disease-modifying treatment, so meaningful benefit-risk needs careful context.
metricGrades.observedResult: ACACIA-HCM NCT06081894 prespecified KCCQ-CSS 36-week aficamten +11.4 vs placebo +8.4, adjusted mean difference +3.0 points (95% CI +0.5 to +5.5; P=0.02). NYHA functional class improvement occurred in 41.9% active vs 27.8% placebo, difference +14.1 percentage points (95% CI 6.0 to 22.2).
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Individual KCCQ changes around 5/10/20 points are often interpreted small/moderate/large; a mean between-group difference of three points is not a comparable within-person change and cannot be promoted to a five-point individual responder benefit.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: KCCQ-CSS group contrast is relatively small and placebo improved substantially. NYHA class responder evidence supports functioning but needs patient-level distribution, missingness and multiplicity context.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: FDA could deem clinical magnitude insufficient despite formal statistical success; do not infer significance for LAVI or clinical events.
metricGrades.observedResult: Both dual co-primary nHCM outcomes were reported at 36 weeks as positive with 95% CI excluding zero: KCCQ-CSS +3.0 (0.5, 5.5), P=0.021; pVO2 +0.67 (0.22,1.1), P=0.003. NYHA and biomarker secondaries favorable; left atrial volume index P=0.058 and time to first cardiovascular event P=0.678 were not significant.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: FDA guidance emphasizes prospective error control for multiple primary/secondary endpoints. ACACIA declared two parallel primary endpoints with threshold P<=0.025 for each; numerical p-values meet those thresholds, but a summary cannot replace full SAP and missing-data sensitivity.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Prespecified two-primary split alpha does not demonstrate robustness to all missing data, participant exclusions, multiplicity of secondary outcomes or unreported alternative assumptions. Lower bounds of both primary CIs are small.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Cross-phenotype SEQUOIA success does not eliminate nHCM-specific subgroup and durable benefit uncertainty; long-term ejection-fraction safety requires review.
metricGrades.observedResult: ACACIA-HCM NCT06081894 disclosed broadly consistent prespecified subgroups and continued KCCQ gains among remaining participants to 72 weeks; after four-week aficamten washout, KCCQ returned toward placebo. The 36-week peak oxygen and KCCQ improvements occurred in a trial of 517 randomized nHCM patients.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: SEQUOIA-HCM was a randomized trial of the same molecule but obstructive HCM, not a repeat independent randomized nonobstructive HCM pivotal trial. Different diagnoses and different functional baseline make it unfit as a direct nHCM clinical replication.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Open-label/extension completer data are selected and no independent second nHCM Phase3 replication or all prespecified interaction CIs are established in this source. Within-trial long-term improvement is not independent replication.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: The roughly 9.7-point absolute excess in LVEF<50% versus placebo is material for a cardiac myosin inhibitor, especially if mean efficacy benefit is small. Not a prediction of serious HF rates after commercialization.
metricGrades.observedResult: In ACACIA-HCM NCT06081894 reduced LVEF below 50% occurred in 27/258 (10.5%) aficamten vs 2/259 (0.8%) placebo. metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Direct ACACIA within-trial placebo safety comparison is primary. Published 2024 SEQUOIA safety study is prior drug hazard context in obstructive HCM, not a matched nHCM comparator or an approved favorable event-rate threshold.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Event denominators and adjudication matter; trial was not powered to prove a difference in rare serious HF outcomes, and reversible LVEF changes still imply monitoring burden. Precise long-term safety outside trial is unknown.

metricGrades.benchmarkContext: FDA oncology endpoint guidance identifies PFS as a potentially suitable endpoint but its strength depends on scan timing, independent review and benefit-risk. The active-control randomized comparison is stronger than an unmatched historical control.

metricGrades.benchmarkContext: FDA oncology endpoint guidance emphasizes PFS measurement and interpretation rather than equating radiographic delay with patients feeling/functioning/surviving longer. Active comparator gives a relevant standard-of-care reference.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: PFS clinical meaning varies with GIST symptom burden, competing toxicity and censoring. Full OS, pain, patient reported outcomes and crossover analyses were not independently assessed.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: A small p value cannot substitute for a complete independent biostatistical audit; potential sponsor publication selection and scan interval bias remain.

metricGrades.benchmarkContext: FDA final guidance for multiple endpoints expects alpha control of multiple hypothesis families. Reported single primary endpoint p-value and CI substantiate a strong primary result but cannot prove sensitivity robustness across censored patients.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Public ASCO presentation summary lacks independently audited full SAP, detailed censoring by arm, multiplicity for key secondary outcomes, missing-data sensitivity and ITT vs per-protocol stress tests.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Clinical improvement is supported for maintenance of hypertension control among responders, not for all initially enrolled Cushing patients or glycemic control. Mifepristone historic comparison differs by endpoints and population. No regulatory probability, cross-trial ranking, financial upside or 30-metric composite should be inferred. Explicitly retrospective, not a frozen pre-2024 forecast.
metricGrades.observedResult: GRACE NCT03697109 randomized-withdrawal efficacy (published 2026-02-20): among hypertension responders, loss of blood-pressure response occurred in 11/21 (52%) continuing relacorilant versus 19/22 (86%) receiving placebo at week 12. Difference -34 percentage points, OR 0.17 (95% CI 0.04-0.77), P=0.022. The prespecified primary hypertension endpoint was met, but the prespecified design target was a 50 percentage-point contrast; secondary hyperglycemia analyses were not statistically significant.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Published SEISMIC mifepristone Cushing cohort (2012) reported diastolic blood-pressure response in approximately 38% but was open-label, nonrandomized and assessed treatment response, not randomized withdrawal. It establishes patient-important blood-pressure relevance only; no between-program causal superiority comparison or pre-frozen RAAS success threshold is valid.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Randomized-withdrawal population was response enriched following 22 weeks of open-label treatment: 62 randomized overall, 43 evaluable for hypertension endpoint. Missing endpoint values classified as lost response (roughly 23% missing across arms); modified ITT and per-protocol sensitivity analyses still favored relacorilant. Wide OR confidence limits, selection/generalizability, protocol revisions, and unknown longer-term durability prevent strong efficacy calibration.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Improved blood pressure is a health-relevant intermediate outcome, not direct proof of subjective function or survival for Cushing patients.
metricGrades.observedResult: GRACE NCT03697109 randomized-withdrawal hypertension responders: loss of BP control 11/21 (52%) on continued relacorilant vs 19/22 (86%) after placebo substitution, 34 percentage points favoring treatment. Ambulatory SBP adjusted between-arm difference -6.5 mmHg (95% CI -11.9 to -1.1; P=0.019) in evaluable paired subset.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: ESC guidance estimates standard BP-drug office effect about 9/5 mmHg and ABPM effect about 5/3 mmHg. This is contextual cardiovascular relevance, not a GRACE-specific validated quality-of-life or Cushing MCID benchmark.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: The cohort was selected for response during prior open-label treatment, so results do not establish population-wide patient benefit. Patient-reported physical function, hospitalization and survival improvement not demonstrated in these randomized data.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Changes to prespecified endpoints can affect confirmatory inference; responder-enriched withdrawal may magnify treatment difference compared to an all-randomized prospective trial.
metricGrades.observedResult: GRACE NCT03697109 hypertension loss primary ITT OR 0.17, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.77, P=0.022 (11/21 vs 19/22). Modified ITT 9/19 vs 15/18 (P=0.029), per-protocol 7/15 vs 15/18 (P=0.032). Trial treated missing week-12 data as loss of response; only 62 total subjects randomized after open-label enrichment.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: GRACE original protocol had two co-primary efficacy endpoints and later specified hypertension-loss primary. FDA expects prospective protection against multiplicity and appropriate missing-data sensitivity. Primary estimates and analyses are concordant but a fully prospective protocol-change audit has not been performed.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Primary analysis and two sensitivity subsets remain conventionally significant, but small n, original co-primary endpoint amendment, and selected study population limit certainty.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: The placebo-substitution design enriches responders, and GRADIENT primary miss is a meaningful counterexample rather than positive independent replication.
metricGrades.observedResult: In GRACE, 11/21 continued relacorilant vs 19/22 placebo-substituted patients lost BP control by week 12, showing a sustained on-treatment contrast in selected patients. Independent GRADIENT NCT04308590 had relacorilant SBP reduction -6.6 versus -2.1 mmHg placebo but the between-group primary comparison was nonsignificant.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: GRACE showed BP responder maintenance during 12-week double-blind withdrawal after 22 weeks of open-label treatment. GRADIENT was a separate blinded study of relacorilant in adrenal hypercortisolism with a nonsignificant placebo-adjusted SBP primary, limiting the replication claim.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: The open-label treatment period and short randomized-withdrawal window do not establish long-term randomized maintenance in all hypercortisolism etiologies. Different etiology and trial design limit direct cross-study reproducibility.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Do not interpret absence of observed endocrine signal as zero future risk or as a controlled safety superiority claim against FDA-approved drugs.
metricGrades.observedResult: GRACE randomized-withdrawal safety: back pain 5/30 versus 6/32, headache 3/30 versus 4/32, acne 3/30 versus 0, bursitis 3/30 versus 0, and withdrawal discontinuation 5/30 versus 5/32. No hypokalemia, adrenal insufficiency, endometrial hypertrophy bleeding, or drug-induced QT prolongation observed in the trial.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: GRACE published arm-level withdrawal AEs in 30 relacorilant vs 32 placebo participants; GRADIENT sponsor reports consistent qualitative tolerability. Neither study directly compares against mifepristone or steroidogenesis inhibitors, and rare-event confidence is limited.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Earlier GRACE open-label stage had 57/152 discontinuations for multiple reasons including AEs and withdrawal. A small selected 12-week randomized population does not establish rare or long-term safety or peer drug superiority.

metricGrades.observedResult: GRADIENT NCT04308590 issuer stated prespecified between-group SBP primary was not statistically significant, even though relacorilant within-arm change was -6.6 mmHg (P=0.012). metricGrades.benchmarkContext: A prespecified placebo-adjusted primary failing significance cannot be replaced by within-arm favorable change or unadjusted positives in several secondary endpoints. Source publication lacks full SAP and imputation analyses.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Missing full primary confidence interval, dropout-adjusted sensitivity and multiplicity hierarchy mean secondary robustness is not settled; known primary miss is an adverse inferential fact rather than an unknown.

metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: GRADIENT 22-week primary is negative, and no subsequent independent adrenal-only confirmation or longer blinded durability has been disclosed, but other relacorilant hypercortisolism subgroup signals exist.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Cardiovascular and infection or tumor-related events require case-by-case adjudication rather than automatic attribution; earlier comparisons are not proof of long-term safety superiority. This is not an FDA safety determination.
metricGrades.observedResult: ClinicalTrials.gov posted GRADIENT NCT04308590 results reported treatment-emergent adverse events through week 26 in 67 of 68 relacorilant patients (98.5%) versus 60 of 69 placebo patients (87.0%). Serious-adverse-event term tables include dyspnoea 2/68 versus 0/69 and acute myocardial infarction 1/68 versus 1/69; these counts are term-level and cannot be summed as unique patients with serious events.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: The direct adverse-event comparison is within GRADIENT NCT04308590: relacorilant n=68 versus placebo n=69, not a cross-trial efficacy or safety comparison. The linked GRACE source concerns another hypercortisolism population and cannot be pooled or treated as an approved medical peer comparator.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: The higher frequency of any TEAE on active treatment is recorded, but treatment causality cannot be established from aggregate event counts. The published source lacks an indication-matched active-treatment peer head-to-head, full per-patient attribution and sufficiently long follow-up to exclude rare harms.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Safety and LVEF monitoring remain vital for a myosin inhibitor. Direct head-to-head is metoprolol only, not mavacamten or all alternatives; no cross-trial treatment ranking, separate FDA regulatory grade or prospective PDUFA odds should be inferred.
metricGrades.observedResult: Exact MAPLE-HCM NCT05767346 double-blind double-dummy 24-week active-control trial randomized 88 aficamten vs 87 metoprolol. Adjusted between-arm peak VO2 change +2.3 mL/kg/min (95% CI +1.5 to +3.1; P<0.001) at primary time point. 2026 prespecified follow-up exercise analysis found >=3.0 mL/kg/min improvements in 20.5% active versus 3.7% metoprolol; metoprolol arm average change was negative.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: MAPLE-HCM planned sample size to detect a 2.0 mL/kg/min aficamten-minus-metoprolol pVO2 difference; its observed point difference +2.3 exceeds that planning assumption, while the 95% lower bound +1.5 remains below 2.0. Separate 2026 oHCM patient-anchor pooled analysis uses these same trial patients and therefore is retrospective contextual evidence, not an independent external clinical validation.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: 175 randomized, 165 (94%) with core-lab validated CPET in later exercise analysis. Some mean contrast arose from deterioration under metoprolol, so superiority to beta blocker does not show equivalence to a placebo comparator or survival impact. Post-hoc/secondary contrasts do not replace the primary prespecified endpoint.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: The comparator was metoprolol monotherapy, not another cardiac myosin inhibitor; do not infer head-to-head superiority to mavacamten or independent survival benefit.
metricGrades.observedResult: MAPLE-HCM NCT05767346 aficamten vs metoprolol at 24 weeks: KCCQ-OSS adjusted mean difference +7.8 points (95% CI +3.3 to +12.3, P=0.001). A >=20-point health status gain occurred in 38.6% vs 18.4% (absolute difference +20.2 points; NNT ~4.9), and deterioration of at least five points occurred in 6.8% vs 18.4%.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: A mean adjusted between-group difference is not itself an individual KCCQ response threshold. The MAPLE patient-level >=20-point outcome was prespecified and offers clinically meaningful responder evidence against an active standard-of-care comparator.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: CI for mean OSS effect includes <5 points and self-reported health status is subjective; adverse outcome differences, missing questionnaire reporting and generalizability to all HCM cases remain relevant.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: An active-control trial could be influenced by effects of comparator on exercise capacity; it cannot prove the same magnitude versus placebo or any other active alternative.
metricGrades.observedResult: MAPLE-HCM NCT05767346 primary between-arm pVO2 +2.3 mL/kg/min (95% CI +1.5 to +3.1; P<0.001); NYHA, KCCQ, LVOT gradient, NT-proBNP and LAVI secondary outcomes favored aficamten, while left ventricular mass index difference was nonsignificant.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: MAPLE reported a blinded prespecified primary pVO2 and secondary outcomes; FDA guidance requires familywise error control and appropriate sensitivity. The randomized active-control report supplies primary confidence intervals and does not substitute for complete SAP.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: A significant primary contrast and consistent secondary outcomes support efficacy, but confidence intervals and multiplicity for every secondary and sensitivity to missing data have not been independently audited as a separate research question.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Effect may be comparator-dependent; no cross-study equivalence or direct comparison with another myosin inhibitor can be inferred.
metricGrades.observedResult: MAPLE NCT05767346 randomized 88 aficamten versus 87 metoprolol with 24-week adjusted peak VO2 difference +2.3 mL/kg/min (95% CI +1.5 to +3.1, P<0.001). The separate SEQUOIA trial reported a 24-week placebo-adjusted +1.7 mL/kg/min, 95% CI +1.0 to +2.4.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Both independent randomized trials concern symptomatic obstructive HCM and aficamten, but MAPLE was against metoprolol and SEQUOIA against placebo. Evidence supports replicated direction not identical effect or long-term MAPLE-specific durability.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Positive short-term direction replicated with different controls, but 52-week MAPLE treatment durability, all subgroup interaction CIs, and comparative long-term cardiac safety require more evidence.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Safety profile is neither clearly better nor catastrophically worse versus metoprolol over 24 weeks, but serious events and cardiac contractility warrant caution.
metricGrades.observedResult: MAPLE-HCM NCT05767346: any serious AE 7/88 (8%) aficamten vs 6/87 (6.9%) metoprolol; withdrawal due to AE 1.1% vs 3.4%. LVEF<50% by core laboratory 1/88 versus 0/87, while mean LVEF change was -5.3% active vs -0.5% metoprolol. One sudden death after brief viral illness occurred in aficamten group and requires context, not automatic drug attribution.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: MAPLE randomizes directly against metoprolol. Separate SEQUOIA randomized placebo safety informs known myosin inhibitor reversible LVEF risk, but different comparator and background therapies prohibit an indirect efficacy-safety superiority claim.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Small active-control sample limits risk precision; near-equal serious AE incidence does not prove long-term safety equivalence. Ejection fraction reduction and monitoring burden are substantive risks.

Sponsor reports stratification-adjusted placebo differences 39.3 and 40.3 percentage points with both p<0.0001. Observed current results, not predictions.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: The prospective randomized ABTECT-Maintenance control is 20/192 (10.4%) Week-44 clinical remission; both active arms exceeded placebo by about 39–40 percentage points. Published TRUE NORTH ozanimod maintenance trial had 37.0% versus 18.5% (18.5 percentage points). This published cross-program context is NOT a head-to-head benchmark; differences in patient selection and trial timing prevent any claim of therapeutic superiority.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: The readout is issuer-reported (SEC-filed), detailed prespecified effect confidence intervals, full SAP, ascertainment, and handling of missing data are not fully independently verified. Patients were induction responders re-randomized for maintenance; this is not efficacy in all initiating patients. Cross-program comparator is contextual only.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Patient-reported symptoms and long-term function cannot be presumed from endoscopy alone; steroid-free benefit and sustained responses should be checked in full CSR and label. Histologic definitions and protocol changes may matter.

All reported p<0.0001 in issuer SEC exhibit.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Clinically meaningful UC benefit is defined using validated clinical remission, endoscopic healing and corticosteroid-free remission rather than p-values alone. The published GEMINI 1 randomized maintenance study used clinical remission and mucosal healing as relevant patient-oriented disease-control endpoints. Different programs and populations cannot establish relative drug ranking.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: These are clinically meaningful mucosal and steroid-free measurements, but original public topline lacks complete patient-reported quality-of-life score tables, full multiplicity-adjusted confidence intervals and adjudicated missing-data analyses. Sustained remission compares selected induction remitters.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Risk of overconfidence from exceptionally small p-values, responder re-randomization, incomplete ascertainment details, unverified estimand changes or imperfect multiple-comparison adjustment. Missing information is not imputed as an adverse result.

metricGrades.benchmarkContext: TRUE NORTH reported randomized maintenance remission comparisons and prespecified hierarchical outcomes. This is encouraging but does not disclose all analytic details needed to independently test multiplicitiy and missing-data sensitivity.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Reported p-values and predeclared stratification are not substitutes for accessible final SAP, confidence intervals for all contrasts, imputation, sensitivity analyses or an independently reanalysed dataset. metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Do not treat open-label multiyear exposure as independent controlled confirmation or infer durable benefit for induction nonresponders. Full retention, dropout handling, prespecified subgroup interaction tests and maintenance replication remain unresolved.

metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Prior ABTECT-1 and ABTECT-2 randomized induction datasets met their Week-8 clinical-remission primary endpoint for the 50mg arms (ABTECT-1 21.7% vs 2.5% placebo, ABTECT-2 19.8% vs 6.3%). metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Maintenance durability is measured in a selected responder population; the maintenance phase itself has no separate blinded confirmatory maintenance study in these sources. metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Sponsor-reported primary endpoint has a large estimate but may not capture toxic burden, clinical deterioration or OS. No approval inference from one endpoint.
metricGrades.observedResult: PEAK Phase 3 NCT05208047 (bezuclastinib plus sunitinib vs active comparator sunitinib alone) reported median blinded-independent-review PFS 16.5 vs 9.2 months, HR 0.50 (95% CI 0.39–0.65), p<0.0001. Source is sponsor ASCO release; a meaningful PFS increment in post-imatinib GIST rather than a placebo-only assay.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: FDA oncology endpoint guidance identifies PFS as a potentially suitable endpoint but its strength depends on scan timing, independent review and benefit-risk. The active-control randomized comparison is stronger than an unmatched historical control.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: PFS is not overall survival. Full peer-reviewed participant-level SAP, censoring analyses, intercurrent events, independent radiology audit and long-term OS tradeoffs remain unverified here.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Patient-important net benefit might be smaller or larger than PFS alone; absence of mature OS and tolerability review prevents a high-confidence total clinical importance rating.
metricGrades.observedResult: In post-imatinib advanced GIST, tumor progression and need for later treatment are clinically important; PEAK median PFS improved 7.3 months vs sunitinib active control. Source-reported PFS HR=0.50. Mature overall survival, functional or quality-of-life head-to-head differences are not provided by the NDA acceptance press release.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: FDA oncology endpoint guidance emphasizes PFS measurement and interpretation rather than equating radiographic delay with patients feeling/functioning/surviving longer. Active comparator gives a relevant standard-of-care reference.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: PFS clinical meaning varies with GIST symptom burden, competing toxicity and censoring. Full OS, pain, patient reported outcomes and crossover analyses were not independently assessed.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: A small p value cannot substitute for a complete independent biostatistical audit; potential sponsor publication selection and scan interval bias remain.
metricGrades.observedResult: PEAK primary treatment contrast includes HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.39–0.65, p<0.0001 for progression or death; median 16.5 vs 9.2 months. This source-supported interval excludes HR=1 but is not itself a review of all prespecified endpoints, power or sensitivity analyses.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: FDA final guidance for multiple endpoints expects alpha control of multiple hypothesis families. Reported single primary endpoint p-value and CI substantiate a strong primary result but cannot prove sensitivity robustness across censored patients.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Public ASCO presentation summary lacks independently audited full SAP, detailed censoring by arm, multiplicity for key secondary outcomes, missing-data sensitivity and ITT vs per-protocol stress tests.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Mixed: substantial observed time-to-progression benefit, but a single pivotal cohort and immature/unreported survival cannot establish independent durable survival replication.
metricGrades.observedResult: Median PFS 16.5 months combination vs 9.2 months sunitinib; HR0.50 (95% CI0.39–0.65), p<0.0001; objective response46% vs26%.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Active sunitinib monotherapy comparator; time-to-progression durability in exact PEAK participants, not another KIT-mutant indication or unrelated bezuclastinib study.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: PEAK is a single pivotal combination trial in imatinib-resistant/intolerant GIST. Current sponsor PFS is not OS. Grade 3+ transaminase elevations 10.8% vs 1.4% and treatment-related AE discontinuations 7.4% vs 3.8%; full all-cause SAE table remains missing.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Mixed tolerability is supported by actual comparable hypertension/neutropenia and worse hepatic/withdrawal outcomes; it is not an invented midpoint for the undisclosed all-cause SAE total.
metricGrades.observedResult: PEAK combinationvs sunitinib: Grade3+hypertension29.4%vs27.4%,neutropenia15.2%vs15.4%,ALT/AST10.8%vs1.4%,anemia9.3%vs4.8%,diarrhea7.8%vs7.2%. Related-AE withdrawals7.4%vs3.8%;transaminases led to dose reduction12.7%,discontinuation1.5%,allGrade3resolved,noGrade4.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Active sunitinib control in the same GIST pivotal study; compare similar expected TKI toxicities against increased hepatic/withdrawal burden. Longer combination PFS may alter exposure, so cumulative risks are not exposure-adjusted.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Documented arm-level toxicity and discontinuation facts support this provisional assessment. Full all-cause SAE totals and exposure-adjusted rare-event risks remain unresolved; different periods/populations are not pooled.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Clinical improvement is supported for maintenance of hypertension control among responders, not for all initially enrolled Cushing patients or glycemic control. Mifepristone historic comparison differs by endpoints and population. No regulatory probability, cross-trial ranking, financial upside or 30-metric composite should be inferred. Explicitly retrospective, not a frozen pre-2024 forecast.
metricGrades.observedResult: GRACE NCT03697109 randomized-withdrawal efficacy (published 2026-02-20): among hypertension responders, loss of blood-pressure response occurred in 11/21 (52%) continuing relacorilant versus 19/22 (86%) receiving placebo at week 12. Difference -34 percentage points, OR 0.17 (95% CI 0.04-0.77), P=0.022. The prespecified primary hypertension endpoint was met, but the prespecified design target was a 50 percentage-point contrast; secondary hyperglycemia analyses were not statistically significant.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Published SEISMIC mifepristone Cushing cohort (2012) reported diastolic blood-pressure response in approximately 38% but was open-label, nonrandomized and assessed treatment response, not randomized withdrawal. It establishes patient-important blood-pressure relevance only; no between-program causal superiority comparison or pre-frozen RAAS success threshold is valid.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Randomized-withdrawal population was response enriched following 22 weeks of open-label treatment: 62 randomized overall, 43 evaluable for hypertension endpoint. Missing endpoint values classified as lost response (roughly 23% missing across arms); modified ITT and per-protocol sensitivity analyses still favored relacorilant. Wide OR confidence limits, selection/generalizability, protocol revisions, and unknown longer-term durability prevent strong efficacy calibration.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Improved blood pressure is a health-relevant intermediate outcome, not direct proof of subjective function or survival for Cushing patients.
metricGrades.observedResult: GRACE NCT03697109 randomized-withdrawal hypertension responders: loss of BP control 11/21 (52%) on continued relacorilant vs 19/22 (86%) after placebo substitution, 34 percentage points favoring treatment. Ambulatory SBP adjusted between-arm difference -6.5 mmHg (95% CI -11.9 to -1.1; P=0.019) in evaluable paired subset.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: ESC guidance estimates standard BP-drug office effect about 9/5 mmHg and ABPM effect about 5/3 mmHg. This is contextual cardiovascular relevance, not a GRACE-specific validated quality-of-life or Cushing MCID benchmark.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: The cohort was selected for response during prior open-label treatment, so results do not establish population-wide patient benefit. Patient-reported physical function, hospitalization and survival improvement not demonstrated in these randomized data.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Changes to prespecified endpoints can affect confirmatory inference; responder-enriched withdrawal may magnify treatment difference compared to an all-randomized prospective trial.
metricGrades.observedResult: GRACE NCT03697109 hypertension loss primary ITT OR 0.17, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.77, P=0.022 (11/21 vs 19/22). Modified ITT 9/19 vs 15/18 (P=0.029), per-protocol 7/15 vs 15/18 (P=0.032). Trial treated missing week-12 data as loss of response; only 62 total subjects randomized after open-label enrichment.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: GRACE original protocol had two co-primary efficacy endpoints and later specified hypertension-loss primary. FDA expects prospective protection against multiplicity and appropriate missing-data sensitivity. Primary estimates and analyses are concordant but a fully prospective protocol-change audit has not been performed.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Primary analysis and two sensitivity subsets remain conventionally significant, but small n, original co-primary endpoint amendment, and selected study population limit certainty.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: The placebo-substitution design enriches responders, and GRADIENT primary miss is a meaningful counterexample rather than positive independent replication.
metricGrades.observedResult: In GRACE, 11/21 continued relacorilant vs 19/22 placebo-substituted patients lost BP control by week 12, showing a sustained on-treatment contrast in selected patients. Independent GRADIENT NCT04308590 had relacorilant SBP reduction -6.6 versus -2.1 mmHg placebo but the between-group primary comparison was nonsignificant.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: GRACE showed BP responder maintenance during 12-week double-blind withdrawal after 22 weeks of open-label treatment. GRADIENT was a separate blinded study of relacorilant in adrenal hypercortisolism with a nonsignificant placebo-adjusted SBP primary, limiting the replication claim.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: The open-label treatment period and short randomized-withdrawal window do not establish long-term randomized maintenance in all hypercortisolism etiologies. Different etiology and trial design limit direct cross-study reproducibility.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Do not interpret absence of observed endocrine signal as zero future risk or as a controlled safety superiority claim against FDA-approved drugs.
metricGrades.observedResult: GRACE randomized-withdrawal safety: back pain 5/30 versus 6/32, headache 3/30 versus 4/32, acne 3/30 versus 0, bursitis 3/30 versus 0, and withdrawal discontinuation 5/30 versus 5/32. No hypokalemia, adrenal insufficiency, endometrial hypertrophy bleeding, or drug-induced QT prolongation observed in the trial.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: GRACE published arm-level withdrawal AEs in 30 relacorilant vs 32 placebo participants; GRADIENT sponsor reports consistent qualitative tolerability. Neither study directly compares against mifepristone or steroidogenesis inhibitors, and rare-event confidence is limited.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Earlier GRACE open-label stage had 57/152 discontinuations for multiple reasons including AEs and withdrawal. A small selected 12-week randomized population does not establish rare or long-term safety or peer drug superiority.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Within-arm significance cannot substitute for a randomized between-arm success; nominally positive secondary outcomes do not overturn prespecified primary failure.
metricGrades.observedResult: GRADIENT NCT04308590 randomized 137 adults for 22 weeks. Mean ABPM systolic BP reduced 6.6 mmHg with relacorilant (within-arm P=0.012) and 2.1 mmHg with placebo (within-arm nonsignificant). Issuer explicitly states the primary placebo-adjusted between-arm SBP comparison was NOT statistically significant.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Within-arm ABPM improvement can be meaningful, but the prespecified randomized between-group systolic BP endpoint is the success criterion, not the within-treated-arm P value. ESC guidance contextualizes BP magnitude but is not the trial regulatory threshold.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Full between-arm primary confidence interval and trial SAP were not disclosed; known inferential primary miss remains source documented, while exact possible effect sizes are uncertain.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Potential clinical importance is offset by failed primary and reliance on surrogate rather than directly experienced patient benefit.
metricGrades.observedResult: GRADIENT NCT04308590 showed placebo-adjusted fasting glucose change -22.2 mg/dL (P=0.002), oral glucose tolerance AUC -2.6 h*mmol/L (P=0.046), HbA1c -0.3 percentage point (P=0.019) and body weight -3.9 kg (P=0.0001). Five placebo vs one treated patients needed antihypertensive rescue; prespecified SBP primary comparison was nonsignificant.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: GRADIENT's prespecified between-group SBP primary was nonsignificant, while metabolic and weight secondary comparisons were reported with favorable nominal effects. These surrogate outcomes are potentially patient-important but do not establish patient-reported wellbeing or survival.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Nominal secondary P values may not be familywise significant after a failed primary; no independently verified patient QoL or hard health outcome is established.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Post-hoc replacement of a failed primary with secondary outcomes would inflate false-positive conclusions and overstate statistical certainty.
metricGrades.observedResult: GRADIENT NCT04308590 issuer stated prespecified between-group SBP primary was not statistically significant, even though relacorilant within-arm change was -6.6 mmHg (P=0.012). Nominal placebo-adjusted fasting glucose P=0.002 and body-weight P=0.0001 were favorable but are secondary.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: A prespecified placebo-adjusted primary failing significance cannot be replaced by within-arm favorable change or unadjusted positives in several secondary endpoints. Source publication lacks full SAP and imputation analyses.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Missing full primary confidence interval, dropout-adjusted sensitivity and multiplicity hierarchy mean secondary robustness is not settled; known primary miss is an adverse inferential fact rather than an unknown.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Do not transfer GRACE benefit to GRADIENT adrenal population or treat glucose/weight secondary signals as replicated BP-primary success.
metricGrades.observedResult: GRADIENT NCT04308590 sponsor reported no statistically significant difference between relacorilant and placebo on prespecified ambulatory SBP primary, despite within-relacorilant -6.6 mmHg versus placebo -2.1 mmHg and favorable glucose/weight secondary outcomes. GRACE NCT03697109 documented maintenance of hypertension control during 12-week blinded withdrawal in patients previously responding.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: GRACE responder-enriched double-blind withdrawal and GRADIENT placebo-controlled adrenal etiology have clinically nonexchangeable populations and endpoints; GRACE positive BP maintenance is context, not GRADIENT efficacy replication.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: GRADIENT 22-week primary is negative, and no subsequent independent adrenal-only confirmation or longer blinded durability has been disclosed, but other relacorilant hypercortisolism subgroup signals exist.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Cardiovascular and infection or tumor-related events require case-by-case adjudication rather than automatic attribution; earlier comparisons are not proof of long-term safety superiority. This is not an FDA safety determination.
metricGrades.observedResult: ClinicalTrials.gov posted GRADIENT NCT04308590 results reported treatment-emergent adverse events through week 26 in 67 of 68 relacorilant patients (98.5%) versus 60 of 69 placebo patients (87.0%). Serious-adverse-event term tables include dyspnoea 2/68 versus 0/69 and acute myocardial infarction 1/68 versus 1/69; these counts are term-level and cannot be summed as unique patients with serious events.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: The direct adverse-event comparison is within GRADIENT NCT04308590: relacorilant n=68 versus placebo n=69, not a cross-trial efficacy or safety comparison. The linked GRACE source concerns another hypercortisolism population and cannot be pooled or treated as an approved medical peer comparator.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: The higher frequency of any TEAE on active treatment is recorded, but treatment causality cannot be established from aggregate event counts. The published source lacks an indication-matched active-treatment peer head-to-head, full per-patient attribution and sufficiently long follow-up to exclude rare harms.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Safety and LVEF monitoring remain vital for a myosin inhibitor. Direct head-to-head is metoprolol only, not mavacamten or all alternatives; no cross-trial treatment ranking, separate FDA regulatory grade or prospective PDUFA odds should be inferred.
metricGrades.observedResult: Exact MAPLE-HCM NCT05767346 double-blind double-dummy 24-week active-control trial randomized 88 aficamten vs 87 metoprolol. Adjusted between-arm peak VO2 change +2.3 mL/kg/min (95% CI +1.5 to +3.1; P<0.001) at primary time point. 2026 prespecified follow-up exercise analysis found >=3.0 mL/kg/min improvements in 20.5% active versus 3.7% metoprolol; metoprolol arm average change was negative.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: MAPLE-HCM planned sample size to detect a 2.0 mL/kg/min aficamten-minus-metoprolol pVO2 difference; its observed point difference +2.3 exceeds that planning assumption, while the 95% lower bound +1.5 remains below 2.0. Separate 2026 oHCM patient-anchor pooled analysis uses these same trial patients and therefore is retrospective contextual evidence, not an independent external clinical validation.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: 175 randomized, 165 (94%) with core-lab validated CPET in later exercise analysis. Some mean contrast arose from deterioration under metoprolol, so superiority to beta blocker does not show equivalence to a placebo comparator or survival impact. Post-hoc/secondary contrasts do not replace the primary prespecified endpoint.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: The comparator was metoprolol monotherapy, not another cardiac myosin inhibitor; do not infer head-to-head superiority to mavacamten or independent survival benefit.
metricGrades.observedResult: MAPLE-HCM NCT05767346 aficamten vs metoprolol at 24 weeks: KCCQ-OSS adjusted mean difference +7.8 points (95% CI +3.3 to +12.3, P=0.001). A >=20-point health status gain occurred in 38.6% vs 18.4% (absolute difference +20.2 points; NNT ~4.9), and deterioration of at least five points occurred in 6.8% vs 18.4%.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: A mean adjusted between-group difference is not itself an individual KCCQ response threshold. The MAPLE patient-level >=20-point outcome was prespecified and offers clinically meaningful responder evidence against an active standard-of-care comparator.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: CI for mean OSS effect includes <5 points and self-reported health status is subjective; adverse outcome differences, missing questionnaire reporting and generalizability to all HCM cases remain relevant.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: An active-control trial could be influenced by effects of comparator on exercise capacity; it cannot prove the same magnitude versus placebo or any other active alternative.
metricGrades.observedResult: MAPLE-HCM NCT05767346 primary between-arm pVO2 +2.3 mL/kg/min (95% CI +1.5 to +3.1; P<0.001); NYHA, KCCQ, LVOT gradient, NT-proBNP and LAVI secondary outcomes favored aficamten, while left ventricular mass index difference was nonsignificant.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: MAPLE reported a blinded prespecified primary pVO2 and secondary outcomes; FDA guidance requires familywise error control and appropriate sensitivity. The randomized active-control report supplies primary confidence intervals and does not substitute for complete SAP.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: A significant primary contrast and consistent secondary outcomes support efficacy, but confidence intervals and multiplicity for every secondary and sensitivity to missing data have not been independently audited as a separate research question.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Effect may be comparator-dependent; no cross-study equivalence or direct comparison with another myosin inhibitor can be inferred.
metricGrades.observedResult: MAPLE NCT05767346 randomized 88 aficamten versus 87 metoprolol with 24-week adjusted peak VO2 difference +2.3 mL/kg/min (95% CI +1.5 to +3.1, P<0.001). The separate SEQUOIA trial reported a 24-week placebo-adjusted +1.7 mL/kg/min, 95% CI +1.0 to +2.4.
metricGrades.benchmarkContext: Both independent randomized trials concern symptomatic obstructive HCM and aficamten, but MAPLE was against metoprolol and SEQUOIA against placebo. Evidence supports replicated direction not identical effect or long-term MAPLE-specific durability.
metricGrades.uncertaintyReview: Positive short-term direction replicated with different controls, but 52-week MAPLE treatment durability, all subgroup interaction CIs, and comparative long-term cardiac safety require more evidence.

metricGrades.criticalRiskReview: Safety profile is neither clearly better nor catastrophically worse versus metoprolol over 24 weeks, but serious events and cardiac contractility warrant caution.
